Printed inconsistencies kept verbatim: decimal commas in 'T_3 = 372,65 K', '5,0 cm^3' and '99,6 kPa' amid decimal points; V_w3 is printed as 62.6 cm^3 in A.4 but 62.5 ml in B.4; the kelvin symbol in B.2 is printed in italic ('372.65 K'); 'ln' is printed in italic in several formulas; A.2 solution says '(air and air vapor mixture)'. problems.title: Problem 2: Coffee - Flavored Physics

figures.caption: Fig. 1
figures.alt: Photo of an assembled red moka pot with labels: “collector” on the upper vessel, “kettle” on the lower part, and an arrow marking the “safety valve” on the kettle.

figures.caption: Fig. 2
figures.alt: Photo of the disassembled moka pot: the collector (top, upside down with handle), the funnel with its coffee container (middle, labelled “funnel” with an arrow) and the kettle (bottom).

figures.caption: Fig. 3
figures.alt: Photo of the underside of the collector showing the perforated filter surrounded by the rubber gasket, next to the funnel’s container with its perforated base; labels “rubber gasket” and “perforated discs” with arrows.

figures.caption: Fig. 4
figures.alt: Schematic cross-section of the kettle (red walls) with water (cyan) up to a level below the funnel’s container; the funnel tube dips into the water; the container on top holds “ground coffee”; the spaces between the funnel and the kettle walls above the water are labelled “air pocket”; labels “safety valve” (orange square on the left wall), “funnel” and “water”.

parts.label: A.1
parts.statement:
**Water vapors (0.9 p)**

Above the water in the kettle, trapped between the wall of the funnel and that of the kettle, there is a fixed amount of air and a variable quantity of saturated water vapors – the so-called ”air pocket” in Fig. 4. Knowing that the mass of water vaporized during the heating process is negligible compared with the total mass of water, derive an expression for the mass of saturated water vapors ($m_{sv,2}$) in the air pocket at the temperature $\theta_2 = 72.0\ {}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and calculate its numerical value. The molar mass for water is $\mu_w = 18.0\ \mathrm{g/mol}$, the ideal gas constant is $R = 8.32\ \mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}$.

parts.label: A.2
parts.statement:
**The initial volume of the air pocket (0.8 p)**

When the water temperature reaches $\theta_2 = 72.0\ {}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the level difference between the water in the funnel and that in the kettle is $\Delta h = 12.1\ \mathrm{mm}$. Derive an expression for the volume of the air pocket ($V_{air,1}$) in the initial state (at $\theta = \theta_1$) and calculate its numerical value. The gravitational acceleration is $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.

parts.label: A.3
parts.statement:
**The internal energy variation (1.4 p)**

Determine a mathematical expression for the internal energy variation of the air trapped in the air pocket ($\Delta U_{air/air\ pocket}$), as well as for that of the air in the collector ($\Delta U_{air/collector}$), during the $\theta_1 \to \theta_2$ heating process, and calculate their numerical values. The average specific heat of air at constant volume for the temperature range of interest is $c_V = 719\ \mathrm{J/(kg\cdot K)}$ and the molar mass of air is $\mu_{air} = 29.0\ \mathrm{g/mol}$.

answer.value: ΔU_air/airpocket = m_air c_V (T_2 − T_1) = 0.566 J; ΔU_air/collector = C_V (n_2 T_2 − n_1 T_1) = 0 J

parts.label: A.4
parts.statement:
**The pressure in the air pocket at the end of stage one (1.1 p)**

As the temperature rises from $\theta_2 = 72.0\ {}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ to $\theta_3 = 99.5\ {}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, the water is flooding the coffee plug which fills the container of the funnel. The coffee plug has the mass $m_c = 6.0\ \mathrm{g}$ and the density of compacted coffee is $\rho_c = 1190\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$. At $\theta_3 = 99.5\ {}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ the water fills completely the container and this is the end of stage one of coffee brewing. Derive an expression for the pressure $p_3$ above the water in the kettle at $\theta_3 = 99.5\ {}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and calculate its numerical value. For the purpose of this task, neglect the solubility of any coffee component in water, as well as the mass of the water vapors with respect to the total mass of water.

answer.note: Printed: p_3 = 42 kPa + 99.6 kPa = 141.6 kPa ≅ 1.4·10^2 kPa.

parts.statementAfter:
**B. Stage two: the rise of the water in the collector (5.8 p)**

This process takes place at the constant temperature $\theta = \theta_3$. The water starts flowing through the filter once the container of the funnel is filled with water and the driver of this process is the pressure difference at the ends of the filter. After the water is transferred to the collector, this second stage of functioning of the moka pot is over. The well-known gurgling sound signals that the coffee brewing is finished.

parts.label: B.1
parts.statement:
**The filtration law (0.7 p)**

When the container of the funnel is loaded with ground coffee, the coffee plug (together with the bordering perforated Al discs) will act as a cylindrical filter, the properties of which will depend on the dimensions of the coffee grains and the compactness of the coffee plug. The filtration law gives the relationship between the volume flow rate $Q$ of water through the filter and the pressure difference $\Delta p$ on its faces and is similar with Ohm’s law in electricity. The hydrodynamic resistance of the filter $\mathcal{R}_h$, similarly to its counterpart in electricity, depends on the area $S$ of the plug’s transversal section, its height $h$, but it also depends on the dynamic viscosity coefficient $\eta$ of water and on the so-called filtration coefficient, $k$, also known as the permeability of the filter. Knowing that the filtration coefficient has the dimension of an area and that the measurement unit for $\eta$ in SI is $\mathrm{Pa\cdot s}$, derive an expression for $\mathcal{R}_h$, as a function of $S, h, k$ and $\eta$, using dimensional analysis. Consider any numeric coefficient equal to one.

parts.label: B.2
parts.statement:
**Time evolution of air pressure in the air pocket (1.4 p)**

Derive the variation law for the pressure of the air in the air pocket during the second stage of the functioning cycle of the moka pot, as a function of time, $p_{air}(t)$. For simplicity, consider that the hydrodynamic resistance of the filter is constant during this stage.

parts.label: B.3
parts.statement:
**The hydrodynamic resistance of the filter filled with coffee (0.7 p)**

When the container is filled with ground coffee, the water passage through the filter takes the time $\tau_c = 54\ \mathrm{s}$. Derive an expression for the hydrodynamic resistance of the filter filled with ground coffee ($\mathcal{R}_h$) and calculate its numerical value.

parts.label: B.4
parts.statement:
**The filtration coefficient of the coffee plug (1.2 p)**

When the funnel’s container is empty, the passage time of the same quantity of water through this filter is $\tau_0 = 17\ \mathrm{s}$ and the water transfer through the funnel takes place at the same temperature as in the presence of the coffee plug. Derive an expression for the filtration coefficient of coffee ($k$) and calculate its numerical value. Assume that the water reaches the base of the funnel’s container at the same temperature as above, even if the coffee plug is absent. When the coffee plug is in the container, consider that all the water passing the filter goes through coffee.

parts.label: B.5
parts.statement:
**The work done by the air pocket during the coffee filtration process (0.8 p)**

Derive an expression for the work done by the air ($\mathcal{W}_{air}$) from the air pocket, as well as for the work done by the water saturated vapors ($\mathcal{W}_{sv}$) from the air pocket, respectively, on the water inside the kettle during the filtration process and calculate their numerical values.

answer.value: W_air = p_air3 V_air3 ln(V_0/V_air3) = 1.3 J; W_sv = p_sv,3 (V_0 − V_air3) = 4.7 J

parts.label: B.6
parts.statement:
**The work done for circulating the water through the filter to produce coffee infusion (1.0 p)**

Derive an expression for the work done to pass the water from the kettle through the filter ($\mathcal{W}_w$) and calculate its numerical value.

problems.statementAfterParts:
***Note:*** *If needed, you can use one of the following pieces of information:*

$$\ln(1 + x) \cong x - \frac{x^2}{2}$$

*The relative error made for the above approximation is below* $1\%$ *for* $x < 0.177$.

$$\int \frac{dx}{x^2(x + a)} = \frac{1}{a^2}\left[ln\left(1 + \frac{a}{x}\right) - \frac{a}{x}\right] + \mathcal{C}$$

$$\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{1 + ax}} = \frac{2}{a}\sqrt{1 + ax} + \mathcal{C}$$

$$\int \frac{dx}{1 + ax} = \frac{1}{a}\ln\left(1 + ax\right) + \mathcal{C}$$

**Assoc. Prof. Sebastian POPESCU, PhD**

*Faculty of Physics, Alexandru Ioan Cuza University of Iasi, ROMANIA*

solution.statement:
**A.1 Water vapors (0.9 p)**

**Solution:** **0.9 p**

The mass of saturated water vapors in the air pocket at the temperature $\theta_2$ is

$$m_{sv,2} = \rho_{sv,2}V_{air,2},$$

**0.1 p**

where

$$\rho_{sv,2} = \frac{p_{sv,2}\mu_w}{RT_2}$$

**0.2 p**

$$\left(\rho_{sv,2} = 0.213\ \frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^3}\right)$$

and the volume occupied by air at $\theta_2 = 72.0\ {}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is

$$V_{air,2} = V_0 - V_{w2},$$

**0.1 p**

where

$$V_{w2} = \frac{m_w}{\rho_{w2}}$$

**0.1 p**

$$\left(V_{w2} = 61.4\ \mathrm{cm}^3 \text{ and } V_{air,2} = 22.8\ \mathrm{cm}^3\right),$$

because the mass of water vaporized in this process is negligible compared with the total mass of water.

Hence,

$$\boxed{m_{sv,2} = \frac{p_{sv,2}\mu_w}{RT_2}\left(V_0 - \frac{m_w}{\rho_{w2}}\right)},$$

**0.2 p**

having the numerical value

$$\boxed{m_{sv,2} = 4.86\cdot 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{g}},$$

**0.2 p**

which is, indeed, negligible compared to the mass of water.

**A.2 The initial volume of the air pocket (0.8 p)**

**Solution:** **0.8 p**

The air pocket volume at the beginning of the heating stage can be obtained from the general transformation equation of an ideal gas

$$\frac{p_{air,1}V_{air,1}}{T_1} = \frac{p_{air,2}V_{air,2}}{T_2},$$

hence

$$V_{air,1} = \frac{p_{air,2}}{p_{air,1}}\frac{T_1}{T_2}V_{air,2}.$$

**0.2 p**

Initially, the pressure in the air pocket (air and air vapor mixture) is the atmospheric pressure, so

$$p_{air1} = p_{air}(T_1) = p_0 - p_{sv,1}$$

**0.1 p**

$$\left(p_{air1} = 96.4\ \mathrm{kPa} - 1.98\ \mathrm{kPa} = 94.4\ \mathrm{kPa}\right).$$

In the state 2,

$$p_{air2} = p_{air}(T_2) = (p_0 + \rho_{w2}g\Delta h) - p_{sv,2}$$

**0.1 p**

$$\left(p_{air2} = (96.4\ \mathrm{kPa} + 116\ \mathrm{Pa}) - 34.0\ \mathrm{kPa} = 62.5\ \mathrm{kPa}\right).$$

Hence

$$\boxed{V_{air,1} = \frac{p_0 + \rho_{w2}g\Delta h - p_{sv,2}}{p_0 - p_{sv,1}}\frac{T_1}{T_2}\left(V_0 - \frac{m_w}{\rho_{w2}}\right)}$$

**0.2 p**

and its numerical value is

$$\boxed{V_{air,1} = \frac{62.5}{94.4}\times\frac{290.45}{345.15}\times 22.8\ \mathrm{cm}^3 = 12.7\ \mathrm{cm}^3}.$$

**0.2 p**

**A.3 The internal energy variation (1.4 p)**

**Solution:** **1.4 p**

In the kettle:

The air pocket is a closed system. The mass of air is

$$m_{air} = \frac{p_{air,1}V_{air,1}\mu_{air}}{RT_1}$$

**0.2 p**

$$\left(m_{air} = 1.44\cdot 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{kg}\right),$$

so, the internal energy variation is

$$\boxed{\Delta U_{air/airpocket} = m_{air}c_V(T_2 - T_1)},$$

**0.2 p**

having the numerical value

$$\boxed{\Delta U_{air/airpocket} = 0.566\ \mathrm{J}}.$$

**0.2 p**

In the collector:

Because the collector is not sealed, the air volume is an open system, so, at any temperature, the Clapeyron-Mendeleev equation is

$$p_0V_{collector} = nRT,$$

because the air in the collector is permanently at atmospheric pressure. Since $V_{collector}$ is also constant, under the assumption that the thermal dilatation of the pot is neglected, then, at any temperature we will have

$$nT = const.$$

**0.3 p**

The internal energy variation of the air from the collector is

$$\Delta U_{air/collector} = U_{air/collector,2} - U_{air/collector,1} = (n_2C_VT_2 + U_0) - (n_1C_VT_1 + U_0),$$

**0.2 p**

so

$$\boxed{\Delta U_{air/collector} = C_V(n_2T_2 - n_1T_1)},$$

**0.2 p**

having the numerical value

$$\boxed{\Delta U_{air/collector} = 0\ \mathrm{J}}.$$

**0.1 p**

**A.4 The pressure in the air pocket at the end of stage one (1.1 p)**

**Solution:** **1.1 p**

The pressure above the water in the kettle is

$$p_3 = p_{air,3} + p_{sv,3},$$

**0.1 p**

where

$$p_{air,3} = \frac{T_3}{T_2}\frac{V_{air,2}}{V_{air,3}}p_{air,2}.$$

**0.2 p**

$$\left(p_{air,3} = 41.6\ \mathrm{kPa} \cong 42\ \mathrm{kPa}\right).$$

The air volume trapped in the kettle at $T_3 = 372{,}65\ \mathrm{K}$ is

$$V_{air,3} = V_0 - \left(V_{w3} - V_f\right),$$

**0.1 p**

where the water volume is

$$V_{w3} = \frac{m_w}{\rho_{w3}}$$

**0.1 p**

$$\left(V_{w3} = 62.6\ \mathrm{cm}^3\right)$$

and the container volume flooded by water is

$$V_f = \frac{\pi d^2h}{4} - \frac{m_c}{\rho_c}.$$

**0.2 p**

$$\left(V_f = 20\ \mathrm{cm}^3 - 5{,}0\ \mathrm{cm}^3 = 15.0\ \mathrm{cm}^3 \cong 15\ \mathrm{cm}^3 \text{ and } V_{air,3} = 36.6\ \mathrm{cm}^3 \cong 37\ \mathrm{cm}^3\right).$$

So,

$$\boxed{p_3 = \frac{T_3}{T_2}\frac{V_0 - \frac{m_w}{\rho_{w2}}}{V_0 - \frac{m_w}{\rho_{w3}} + \frac{\pi d^2h}{4} - \frac{m_c}{\rho_c}}\left(p_0 + \rho_{w2}g\Delta h - p_{sv,2}\right) + p_{sv,3}},$$

**0.2 p**

its numerical value being

$$\boxed{p_3 = 42\ \mathrm{kPa} + 99.6\ \mathrm{kPa} = 141.6\ \mathrm{kPa} \cong 1.4\cdot 10^2\ \mathrm{kPa}}.$$

**0.2 p**

**B.1 The filtration law (0.7 p)**

**Solution:** **0.7 p**

The filtration law is

$$\Delta p = Q\cdot\mathcal{R}_h$$

**0.2 p**

and

$$\mathcal{R}_h = f(\eta, k)\frac{h}{S},$$

**0.2 p**

because, in electricity, the electric resistance can be written as

$$R = \rho\frac{l}{S},$$

where $\rho$ is the electric resistivity of the given resistor.

Then, using dimensional analysis, it follows that

$$\mathcal{R}_h = C\eta^{\alpha}k^{\beta}hS^{-1},$$

**0.1 p**

with

$$C = 1,$$

as stated in the text.

According to the details in the following table, giving the physical quantities, their measurement units in SI and their dimensions

| X | $\mathcal{R}_h$ | $S$ | $h$ | $\eta$ | $k$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\langle X\rangle_{\mathrm{SI}}$ | $\mathrm{Pa}\cdot\frac{\mathrm{s}}{\mathrm{m}^3} = \frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}^4\mathrm{s}}$ | $\mathrm{m}^2$ | $\mathrm{m}$ | $\mathrm{Pa}\cdot\mathrm{s} = \frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m}\cdot\mathrm{s}}$ | $\mathrm{m}^2$ |
| $[X]$ | $\mathrm{L}^{-4}\mathrm{MT}^{-1}$ | $\mathrm{L}^2$ | $\mathrm{L}$ | $\mathrm{L}^{-1}\mathrm{MT}^{-1}$ | $\mathrm{L}^2$ |

the dimensional equation will be:

$$\mathrm{L}^{-4}\mathrm{MT}^{-1} = \left(\mathrm{L}^{-1}\mathrm{MT}^{-1}\right)^{\alpha}\mathrm{L}^{2\beta}\mathrm{L}\cdot\mathrm{L}^{-2},$$

or, equating the exponents,

$$\begin{cases} \alpha = 1 \\ \beta = -1 \end{cases},$$

hence

$$\boxed{\mathcal{R}_h = \frac{\eta h}{kS}}.$$

**0.2 p**

**B.2 Time evolution of air pressure in the air pocket (1.4 p)**

**Solution:** **1.4 p**

The water flowing equation is

$$p_{air} + p_{sv,3} - p_0 = \mathcal{R}_hQ.$$

**0.1 p**

Denoting

$$a = p_{sv,3} - p_0 = 3.2\ \mathrm{kPa},$$

the above equation can be written as

$$p_{air} + a = -\mathcal{R}_h\frac{dV}{dt},$$

**0.2 p**

because the water volume in the kettle decreases in time.

The second stage is, essentially, an isothermal process at $T_3 = 372.65\ K$, for which the air volume is

$$V_0 - V = \frac{p_{air3}V_{air3}}{p_{air}},$$

**0.2 p**

where $V$ is the volume occupied by water at that instant.

Hence

$$-\frac{dV}{dt} = -\frac{p_{air3}V_{air3}}{p_{air}^2}\frac{dp_{air}}{dt},$$

**0.1 p**

which gives

$$p_{air} + a = -\mathcal{R}_h\frac{p_{air3}V_{air3}}{p_{air}^2}\frac{dp_{air}}{dt}.$$

**0.2 p**

After separating the variables, we get

$$\frac{dp_{air}}{p_{air}^2(p_{air} + a)} = -\frac{dt}{\mathcal{R}_hp_{air3}V_{air3}}.$$

Using the integral given at the end of the text, it follows that

$$\frac{1}{a^2}\left[ln\left(1 + \frac{a}{p_{air}}\right) - \frac{a}{p_{air}}\right] = -\frac{t}{\mathcal{R}_hp_{air3}V_{air3}} + \mathcal{C}.$$

**0.2 p**

Since $a = 3.2\ \mathrm{kPa}$ and $p_{air}$ varies between $p_{air3} = 42\ \mathrm{kPa}$ and $p_{air4} = \frac{p_{air3}V_{air3}}{V_0} = 18.5\ \mathrm{kPa} \cong 19\ \mathrm{kPa}$, this means that the ratio $\frac{a}{p_{air}}$ varies between 0.076 and 0.17. Consequently, the logarithm function can be approximated as suggested at the end of the text

$$\ln(1 + x) \cong x - \frac{x^2}{2},\ \text{for } x < 0.177,$$

so, the above equation can be written as

$$\frac{1}{2p_{air}^2} = \frac{t}{\mathcal{R}_hp_{air3}V_{air3}} - \mathcal{C}.$$

**0.1 p**

The integration constant can be determined considering that at $t = 0 \to\ p_{air} = p_{air3}$, so

$$\mathcal{C} = -\frac{1}{2p_{air3}^2}.$$

**0.1 p**

As a result,

$$\boxed{p_{air}(t) = p_{air3}\left(1 + \frac{2p_{air3}t}{\mathcal{R}_hV_{air3}}\right)^{-1/2}}.$$

**0.2 p**

**B.3 The hydrodynamic resistance of the filter filled with coffee (0.7 p)**

**Solution:** **0.7 p**

At the end of the stage two, the air pressure in the kettle is $p_{air4}$ (with the numerical value given above), so

$$\mathcal{R}_h = \frac{2p_{air3}\tau_c}{V_{air3}\left[\left(\frac{p_{air3}}{p_{air4}}\right)^2 - 1\right]}.$$

**0.1 p**

Since

$$p_{air4} = \frac{p_{air3}V_{air3}}{V_0},$$

**0.2 p**

then

$$\boxed{\mathcal{R}_h = \frac{2p_{air3}\tau_c}{V_{air3}\left[\left(\frac{V_0}{V_{air3}}\right)^2 - 1\right]}}.$$

**0.2 p**

Its numerical value is

$$\boxed{\mathcal{R}_h = 2.9\cdot 10^{10}\ \mathrm{Pa\cdot s\cdot m^{-3}}}.$$

**0.2 p**

**B.4 The filtration coefficient of the coffee plug (1.2 p)**

**Solution:** **1.2 p**

From the text, states 1 and 2 are the same, while the state 3 becomes 3’, characterized by

$$V'_{air,3} = V_0 - (V_{w3} - V_{container}) = 84.2\ \mathrm{ml} - 62.5\ \mathrm{ml} + 20\ \mathrm{ml} = 41.7\ \mathrm{ml} \cong 42\ \mathrm{ml}.$$

**0.1 p**

and

$$p'_3 = p'_{air,3} + p_{sv,3},$$

where

$$p'_{air,3} = \frac{T_3}{T_2}\frac{V_{air,2}}{V'_{air,3}}p_{air,2} = 37\ \mathrm{kPa}.$$

**0.2 p**

So

$$p'_3 = 37\ \mathrm{kPa} + 99{,}6\ \mathrm{kPa} = 136.6\ \mathrm{kPa} \cong 1.4\cdot 10^2\ \mathrm{kPa}.$$

Since the transformation 3 → 4, respectively 3’ → 4’ are isothermal, for the same quantity of air, at the same temperature, and with the same final volume, it means that

$$p'_{air4} = p_{air4} = 19\ \mathrm{kPa}.$$

Then

$$\mathcal{R}_{h0} = \frac{2p'_{air3}\tau_0}{V'_{air,3}\left[\left(\frac{V_0}{V'_{air,3}}\right)^2 - 1\right]},$$

**0.1 p**

having the numerical value

$$\mathcal{R}_{h0} = 9.9\cdot 10^9\ \mathrm{Pa\cdot s\cdot m^{-3}}.$$

**0.1 p**

Because

$$R_h = R_{h0} + R_{h,coffee},$$

**0.2 p**

then

$$R_{h,coffee} = 1.9\cdot 10^{10}\ \mathrm{Pa\cdot s\cdot m^{-3}}.$$

**0.1 p**

Finally, the filtration coefficient of the used coffee is

$$\boxed{k = \frac{\eta h}{R_{h,coffee}S} = \frac{4\eta h}{\pi d^2R_{h,coffee}}},$$

**0.2 p**

with the numerical value

$$\boxed{k = 1.4\cdot 10^{-13}\ \mathrm{m}^2}.$$

**0.2 p**

**B.5 The work done by the air pocket during the coffee filtration process (0.8 p)**

**Solution:** **0.8 p**

The work done by the air during its isothermal expansion is

$$\boxed{\mathcal{W}_{air} = p_{air3}V_{air3}ln\frac{V_0}{V_{air3}}},$$

**0.2 p**

having the numerical value

$$\boxed{\mathcal{W}_{air} = 1.3\ \mathrm{J}}.$$

**0.2 p**

The work done by the saturated vapors is

$$\boxed{\mathcal{W}_{sv} = p_{sv,3}\Delta V = p_{sv,3}(V_0 - V_{air3})},$$

**0.2 p**

with the numerical value

$$\boxed{\mathcal{W}_{sv} = 99.6\cdot 10^3\ \mathrm{Pa}\times 47\cdot 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}^3 = 4.7\ \mathrm{J}}.$$

**0.2 p**

**B.6 The work done for circulating the water through the filter to produce coffee infusion (1.0 p)**

**Solution:** **1.0 p**

The work done on the water to make it pass through the filter is

$$\mathcal{W}_w = \int_0^{\tau_c}Pdt,$$

**0.2 p**

where $P$ is the power needed for passing the water through the filter

$$P = \frac{(\Delta p)^2}{\mathcal{R}_h} = \frac{(p_{air} + a)^2}{\mathcal{R}_h} = \frac{a^2}{\mathcal{R}_h} + 2a\frac{p_{air}}{\mathcal{R}_h} + \frac{p_{air}^2}{\mathcal{R}_h}.$$

**0.2 p**

Consequently,

$$\mathcal{W}_w = \frac{a^2}{\mathcal{R}_h}\tau_c + \frac{2a}{\mathcal{R}_h}\int_0^{\tau_c}p_{air}dt + \frac{1}{\mathcal{R}_h}\int_0^{\tau_c}p_{air}^2dt$$

**0.1 p**

and using the time evolution law for $p_{air}$, derived at B2, the work is

$$\mathcal{W}_w = \frac{a^2}{\mathcal{R}_h}\tau_c + \frac{2ap_{air3}}{\mathcal{R}_h}\int_0^{\tau_c}\left(1 + \frac{2p_{air3}t}{\mathcal{R}_hV_{air3}}\right)^{-1/2}dt + \frac{p_{air3}^2}{\mathcal{R}_h}\int_0^{\tau_c}\frac{dt}{1 + \frac{2p_{air3}t}{\mathcal{R}_hV_{air3}}}.$$

**0.1 p**

Finally, using the integrals given at the end of the text, the work becomes

$$\boxed{\mathcal{W}_w = \frac{a^2}{\mathcal{R}_h}\tau_c + 2aV_{air3}\left(\sqrt{1 + \frac{2p_{air3}\tau_c}{\mathcal{R}_hV_{air3}}} - 1\right) + \frac{p_{air3}V_{air3}}{2}ln\left(1 + \frac{2p_{air3}\tau_c}{\mathcal{R}_hV_{air3}}\right)}.$$

**0.2 p**

Numerically,

$$\boxed{\mathcal{W}_w = 1.9\cdot 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{J} + 0.30\ \mathrm{J} + 1.3\ \mathrm{J} = 1.6\ \mathrm{J}}.$$

**0.2 p**
